articles.title: The annoying scam that may be hiding in your work calendar
articles.author: Sarah E. Needleman,Ana Altchek,Tim Paradis
articles.content:
When Pete Thomas spots a meeting on his calendar that he doesn't remember scheduling, the startup executive launches a mini investigation.
He searches his inbox for the sender's name, and if that fails, he tries LinkedIn. If Thomas still comes up empty or senses tomfoolery, he'll scan the invitation's contents for odd URLs or other red flags before hitting delete. He's received several in recent months that failed those checks.
"It's a distraction," said Thomas, CTO of Kapwork, a fintech firm in Los Angeles. "You always have to look for context."
As if email and text message scams weren't enough, workers are contending with a growing wave of phishing attempts arriving through their calendars.
In August, calendar-led attacks surged more than tenfold from July, according to a recent study from email security firm Sublime, while a midyear report from Microsoft found that such attacks nearly quadrupled in June from May.
Cybersecurity pros say calendars offer attackers advantages over more traditional avenues, and that AI is helping to make the schemes more convincing. They also warn that AI agents could give attackers a leg up by accepting fraudulent invitations on workers' behalf.
"You suddenly have new and interesting opportunities because of these personal agents," said Hugh Thompson, program chair of RSAC, an annual cybersecurity conference, and former chief technology officer of software firm Symantec.
Risky business
The goal of most calendar scammers, digital safety experts say, is to lure victims to phishing sites or deploy social engineering attacks that trick people into revealing sensitive information. The tactic is especially problematic for workers in jobs that rely on regularly meeting with strangers online, such as sales, recruiting, consulting, and other client-facing roles.
Aman Gairola, cofounder of Indian design agency Say Design, thought he'd landed a potential client in June when someone booked a meeting on his calendar through his company's website. The invitation included a link to what appeared to be a Google Drive folder containing a project brief.
Gairola said he clicked the link and landed on a page that looked like Google Drive, but something felt off. He checked the URL, saw the site was fake, and stopped short of opening any files.
"If I have to rate this, how convincing it is, I would rate it a 9.5 out of 10," said Gairola, adding that Say Design is considering removing the option to book intro calls directly through its website and switching to a form-based approach. "It has definitely added a layer of scrutiny to the invites that we get."
Attractive vehicles
Calendar invitations are attractive vehicles for scammers in part because they create a sense of urgency, said Mark Beare, an executive at cybersecurity firm Malwarebytes. Workers are common targets since many are used to receiving meeting invitations from colleagues, clients, and partners, he added.
Another allure is that calendar invites are processed differently from standard email attachments, according to the Microsoft report. Malicious links can land on users' calendars without requiring them to explicitly open an attachment, the software giant said.
Calendar invitation scams often take one of two forms. In one, an invitation includes a compromised meeting link, or a form designed to collect credentials or prompt someone to download malware, said Ron Kerbs, CEO of Kidas, which develops tools to detect scams and deepfakes in voice calls.
In the other, he said, a victim joins what appears to be a legit video call, only to encounter a scammer posing as someone they have reason to trust, such as an employee at a real company. The impersonator might use the name of an actual staffer, but a fake email address, as well as AI-generated audio or video to make the ruse more convincing, he said.
"They're using deepfake technology to look the same as the guy from IT," Kerbs said.
Double whammy
Sometimes, the sender really is someone you know.
Scores of Jenn Drummond's contacts recently received an unexpected calendar invitation from her email address, warning that they had been served with a court summons.
The invitation, which was sent after Drummond's email account was hacked while she was boarding a flight, linked to a fake legal notice requesting their financial information.
Drummond, a world-record-setting mountaineer and keynote speaker, said that even if the majority of recipients knew it was a scam, she still feels embarrassed that some people might think she's suing them or that she was hacked in the first place.
"What are people going to think? I'm not trustworthy — and your brand is what you build trust on," Drummond said. "I was sick to my stomach."
Protecting yourself
Cybersecurity veterans say there are limits to what people can reasonably expect to catch. Mathew Woodyard, director of threat intelligence at identity and access management company Okta, said that the burden of securing users mostly falls on the businesses that operate the services.
"The strongest mitigation isn't user education about 'spotting a fake invite,' since the invites increasingly look identical to legitimate ones," he said. "It's giving users something that can't be phished in the first place."
Woodyard said that passkeys can help solve the problem. Because they're created for a specific page, they only work on the authentic website, rather than a mock-up. That removes the need for people to make a judgment call when logging in, Woodyard said.
"Until phishing-resistant factors like passkeys become the default rather than an opt-in afterthought, phishing attacks will keep working," Woodyard said.
Correction: October 12, 2026 — An earlier version of this story misspelled Mathew Woodyard's first name.
articles.summary:
Cybersecurity experts are warning of a significant surge in phishing attacks delivered through calendar invitations, which use deceptive links and AI-generated content to compromise sensitive user information.

### Key Points
- Calendar-based phishing attacks surged more than tenfold in August compared to July, according to data from the security firm Sublime.
- Microsoft reports that these malicious invitations nearly quadrupled between May and June, often bypassing standard email attachment security filters.
- Scammers frequently use fake Google Drive links or impersonate trusted colleagues via deepfake audio and video to steal credentials or deploy malware.
- High-risk roles, including sales, recruiting, and consulting, are primary targets due to their frequent reliance on scheduling meetings with external parties.
- Security professionals recommend adopting phishing-resistant authentication methods, such as passkeys, to prevent unauthorized access to accounts.

### Why it Matters
These sophisticated scams exploit the inherent trust workers place in calendar notifications, creating a new and difficult-to-detect vector for corporate data breaches. As AI tools make these fraudulent invitations increasingly convincing, businesses must shift from relying on user vigilance to implementing robust, phishing-resistant security infrastructure.

articles.title: Ledger confirms hidden chip in crypto wallet amid $92M theft claims
articles.author: Olivia Stephanie
articles.content:
Ledger has confirmed finding an unauthorized hardware implant inside one customer’s cryptocurrency wallet during its October 10 investigation into reported thefts involving Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis, as blockchain researchers estimate suspected losses exceeding $86 million.
- Ledger confirmed an unauthorized hardware implant inside one affected customer’s device during its CryptoBilis investigation.
- CryptoBilis suspended sales of all hardware wallets while Ledger investigates reported losses involving Asian customers.
- Ledger advised customers with CryptoBilis devices against setup and recommended fresh recovery phrases for others.
- Researcher Mark Karpelès reported finding suspicious electronics behind a Ledger Nano X screen in Malaysia.
- Bitquery estimated $92.9 million in cryptocurrency losses across 311 wallets, figures unconfirmed independently by Ledger.
Ledger Support confirmed the discovery in an official statement, saying the modified device belonged to a user affected by the ongoing investigation. The company said CryptoBilis had stopped selling all hardware wallets as a precaution and that Ledger was contacting affected customers while working with authorities. It has not established whether the implant caused the reported cryptocurrency losses.
The discovery provides direct confirmation of physical tampering in at least one device, following earlier warnings about suspicious wallets distributed through the reseller.
Ledger confirms unauthorized implant in customer’s wallet
During its investigation, Ledger identified an additional electronic component inside a wallet belonging to an affected customer.
The company described the component as an “unauthorized hardware implant” but did not disclose the exact device model, how the component was installed or whether it had transmitted any information.
According to Ledger’s October 10 statement, its security team is examining the incident and contacting customers believed to have been affected. The manufacturer has not confirmed how many wallets contain similar modifications.
Reports of unauthorized transactions emerged on October 9 among customers who purchased Ledger products through CryptoBilis, a reseller operating in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. Following the complaints, Ledger opened an investigation into the reported losses and asked the distributor to suspend sales and shipments of its devices.
On-chain investigators had initially identified suspected thefts exceeding $72 million, while another estimate placed the losses above $86 million.
Ledger has not confirmed either amount. The company emphasized in its latest statement that it has found no evidence suggesting its internal security infrastructure, systems or services were compromised.
“We have no indication that Ledger’s security infrastructure, systems or services have been compromised,” the company stated.
The manufacturer is developing additional protections against physical device tampering while investigators work to determine how the unauthorized component entered the affected wallet.
CryptoBilis halts all hardware wallet sales during investigation
Following Ledger’s discovery, CryptoBilis confirmed that it had suspended sales of its entire hardware wallet inventory.
The temporary halt covers all hardware wallet products sold by the distributor, extending beyond the earlier request to pause Ledger sales and shipments.
Meanwhile, CryptoBilis said it will maintain the suspension until the investigation concludes.
Ledger said it remained in active communication with the reseller regarding the investigation and appropriate next steps. Customers who purchased a device through CryptoBilis have been instructed not to begin setting it up if they have not already done so.
For customers who have used the devices, Ledger recommends considering a transfer of their cryptocurrency to a new hardware wallet initialized with a completely new recovery phrase. Moving an existing recovery phrase onto a replacement device would not address possible exposure of that phrase through the original hardware.
Ledger has contacted law enforcement and acknowledged assistance from the Security Alliance’s SEAL_911 incident response initiative.
The company’s statement did not identify any suspects, announce arrests or provide a timetable for completing the investigation. Separately, former CryptoBilis executives Arravind Prabu and Vimalatheethan stated that they had transferred operational control of the business following an ownership change earlier in 2026.
In a statement shared with researcher Mark Karpelès and published by Tibane Labs, the former executives said they completed their management handover in March and no longer controlled company systems or customer databases.
Their statement does not establish who modified the affected device or whether the ownership change had any connection to the incident.
Security researcher reports hidden electronics behind Ledger screen
Before Ledger publicly confirmed the hardware implant, former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès reported examining a suspicious Ledger Nano X device obtained from Malaysia. On October 9, Karpelès described finding an additional electronic component hidden behind the device’s display, inside material normally used to protect the screen.
He reported that the wallet had arrived in packaging that appeared intact, raising questions about whether customers could identify a modified device through a routine visual inspection. In photographs shared publicly, the component appeared to contain electronic circuitry separate from the wallet’s original hardware.
Karpelès subsequently reported examining the modification further and inspecting images provided by other affected users.
A technical account published by Tibane Labs described an arrangement involving a microcontroller, cellular communication hardware and connections to the screen’s internal data lines. The analysis suggested that a component positioned along the screen connection could potentially capture information displayed during wallet setup.
A recovery phrase typically consists of 24 words that allow a wallet owner to restore access to cryptocurrency holdings. If an attacker obtains those words, the attacker may be able to recreate the wallet and authorize transfers without possessing the original hardware device.
Researchers have suggested that an implant capable of reading information sent to the display could potentially capture recovery words when a wallet is initialized.
However, Ledger has not independently confirmed that the discovered implant performed that function or that it was responsible for the reported thefts.
The company’s official announcement confirms physical tampering in one affected device without establishing the technical method used to access customer funds. Ledger’s historical security research has previously examined situations involving unauthorized modifications to wallet hardware.
Ledger urges users to protect recovery phrases
Ledger’s investigation has prompted warnings about the possibility of criminals exploiting public concern surrounding the reseller incident. The company cautioned customers to rely on official communication channels for information about affected devices, investigations and potential security measures. Its public statement reminded customers that Ledger support personnel will never request their 24-word recovery phrase.
Earlier research into fraudulent Ledger websites documented phishing pages that attempted to obtain recovery phrases through fake wallet verification requests.
The report, published October 11, discussed malicious Google advertisements that directed users toward imitation Ledger websites and applications. The phishing campaign has not been linked to the CryptoBilis hardware investigation. In its latest notice, Ledger said it was preparing additional measures intended to make unauthorized physical modifications harder to carry out.
The company did not announce a release date for those protections or provide details of any hardware redesign.
Its security team said affected users would continue receiving direct communication as the investigation proceeds, while information about the incident can be submitted through its bounty program.
articles.summary:
Ledger has confirmed the discovery of an unauthorized hardware implant in a customer’s cryptocurrency wallet following an investigation into significant reported thefts linked to reseller CryptoBilis.

### Key Points
- Ledger identified an unauthorized electronic component inside a wallet during an investigation into reported cryptocurrency losses involving the Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis.
- CryptoBilis has suspended all hardware wallet sales while Ledger and law enforcement investigate the potential security breach.
- Security researcher Mark Karpelès reported finding suspicious circuitry behind the screen of a Ledger Nano X device obtained from Malaysia.
- Blockchain analysis firm Bitquery estimated total losses across 311 affected wallets at approximately $92.9 million, though Ledger has not independently verified this figure.
- Ledger advises customers who purchased devices from CryptoBilis to avoid setup and recommends that existing users transfer assets to new wallets with fresh recovery phrases.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights a critical supply chain vulnerability where physical tampering can compromise hardware wallets before they reach the end user. It underscores the importance of purchasing security devices exclusively through authorized channels to mitigate the risk of sophisticated hardware-level attacks.

articles.title: IMF says AI investment is keeping global growth near 3%
articles.author: Alina Maria Stan
articles.content:
IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday that spending on AI infrastructure is helping the world economy grow by about 3% each year, even though energy prices are high.
She made these comments in Bangkok at the start of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, according to Reuters.
According to Georgieva, Asian economies that produce AI hardware, like Thailand, benefit the most. She estimated that advanced Asian economies could see growth increase by 0.5 to 1 percentage point, while emerging Asian economies might gain 0.2 to 0.8 points.
The scale of that trade is large. In a speech in Singapore last week, Georgieva said AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than a tenth of global trade in goods.
Apart from the US, China, and India, most leading countries in this trade are Asian suppliers of chips, chip-making equipment, and robots.
This demand is rising as major tech companies plan to spend between $660 billion and $690 billion on AI this year.
In its July outlook, the IMF said that AI demand is boosting tech-exporting countries, while conflicts are affecting energy importers. The IMF also predicted 3% growth for 2026.
Georgieva also cautioned about the impact of AI on jobs.
She described AI as a “slow-moving tsunami” that will transform jobs, education, and how governments collect taxes.
According to the Fund, AI will eventually affect about four out of ten jobs worldwide, improving some and making others worse or unnecessary.
Georgieva said, as reported by CNBC, that richer countries are most exposed, with about 60% of jobs affected, compared to 23% in the poorest countries.
Young people entering the job market face the first hit, Georgieva said, because the routine roles they usually start in are disappearing.
Singapore’s President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking on the same panel, said, “The first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand.”
Tharman also warned that if governments do not act, AI could increase the gap in growth and jobs between wealthy and developing countries.
Ajay Banga, the head of the World Bank, said the bank is supporting small AI tools that do not rely on large language models. These tools are designed to help farmers, health systems, and teachers in emerging markets.
The IMF has also pointed out risks from the AI boom. In June, Georgieva warned that Mythos-class AI models could be used to attack the financial system. The Fund will release its updated growth forecasts on Tuesday.

articles.summary:
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva reports that AI infrastructure investment is driving 3% annual global economic growth, with Asian hardware manufacturers seeing the most significant regional gains.

### Key Points
- Global tech companies are projected to spend between $660 billion and $690 billion on AI infrastructure throughout 2024.
- AI-related hardware and technology products now account for more than 10% of total global trade in goods.
- Advanced Asian economies could see growth increase by up to 1 percentage point due to their role in chip and robotics production.
- The IMF estimates that AI will eventually impact 40% of global jobs, with 60% of roles in wealthier nations facing potential transformation.
- The World Bank is currently funding smaller, specialized AI tools to assist farmers, educators, and healthcare systems in emerging markets.

### Why it Matters
The rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is reshaping global trade dynamics and creating a significant economic divide between tech-exporting nations and those reliant on energy imports. While the technology boosts productivity, the displacement of entry-level roles threatens to widen the employment gap between wealthy and developing countries.

articles.title: How Apple can win the smart home
articles.author: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy
articles.content:
This week, Apple is hosting its first-ever dedicated smart home event. While the company hasn’t shared details about what it will reveal at the “Welcome Home experience” in New York City on Tuesday, October 13th, it doesn’t take an army of internet sleuths to deduce we’ll get news about Apple Home — specifically, new hardware. Apple finally seems to be taking the smart home seriously.
How Apple can win the smart home
New hardware could put Apple back in the race, but software will determine whether it wins.
According to Bloomberg, Apple will release a smart home display alongside a refreshed HomePod Mini and Apple TV. The display, which MacRumors reports may be called HomeView, is arguably Apple’s first dedicated Apple Home hardware since it launched the HomeKit platform in 2014. As exciting as this is (and I’ll be there in person to check it out), the real shift will be bringing Siri AI and Apple Intelligence into the home. Apple is years behind Google and Amazon in smart-home hardware, but success in the home depends far more on software. That’s where Apple could leapfrog the competition.
New home hardware is long overdue. Apple announced the HomePod Mini on October 13th, 2020, six years to the day from this week’s event, and the newest Apple TV 4K is now four years old. And those aren’t dedicated smart home devices; they’re more content-consumption gadgets with a side of home automation. The new smart display is reportedly designed to be the heart of Apple Home, marking a complete reboot of the ecosystem, and Apple Home users have wanted it for years.
The smart display category has a bumpy history. Amazon and Google have launched several generations of these voice- and touchscreen-controlled smart speakers that can control smart home gadgets like lights and locks, pull up doorbell camera feeds, and make video calls. But the category has seen very little innovation, and its best use case has been serving as a digital photo frame.
Based on leaks, Apple’s product doesn’t sound that different from what’s come before. According to Bloomberg, it will have a 6-inch square display on a speaker base or as a wall-mounted option, facial recognition to show your personal messages and calendar, a minimalist touchscreen interface to control locks and thermostats, and FaceTime and intercom calls. Nothing groundbreaking, except the rumored price — $350, ouch. The difference has to be in the software and the smart assistant that powers it.
Bloomberg reports the smart display will launch with a brand-new homeOS built around Siri AI. Generative AI has breathed new life into the smart home voice assistant by both making it easier to talk to and expanding its capabilities. Until now, Apple’s new Siri AI has been MIA from its HomePods and Apple TV; when you talk to those, the old Siri responds in its basic, functional way.
Apple is the last of the big three to bring generative AI to its home assistant. Amazon and Google launched theirs last year, but Alexa Plus is only just starting to get it right, and Google’s Gemini for Home, an underpowered version of Gemini, is a confusing mess of capabilities. Now it’s Apple’s turn, and if the company can successfully merge its superpowered personal assistant on your iPhone with a superpowered assistant for your home, it may have a hit on its hands.
That’s a very big if. So far, every company has hit significant roadblocks bringing a smarter assistant to the home. Apple announced Apple Intelligence in 2024, but Siri AI only arrived last month; a version of Alexa Plus was announced in 2023 but didn’t launch until 2025; Gemini for Home is still in an early access program and split into a weird hybrid model where its more capable version, Gemini Live, is restricted from interacting with the home.
These cautious approaches are down to the fact that the home is a big, complicated, messy, multi-user environment that is hard to control. An agentic AI getting something wrong could have consequences far greater than accidentally sending an email. Smart home systems are connected to critical infrastructure like HVAC, locks, and security systems. Every home is different, with unique needs — there is no single plug-and-play solution.
Progress has been made toward solving one of the smart home’s biggest challenges: interoperability, with open standards like Matter and Thread promising to make setting up and using a smart home easier. But these are protocols, not software. It’s the platforms that have to make the smart home work. Here is where Apple may have the edge.
Four years ago, after helping found Matter, Apple rebuilt HomeKit’s underlying architecture and revamped the Home app, laying a strong foundation. That move also let Apple Home work with more devices from more manufacturers (previously, it was limited to those willing to go through the often arduous HomeKit approval process).
However, a smart home isn’t just about the devices you put in it. It’s about making them work together. That’s where Siri AI and Apple Intelligence could play a major role. While Apple used Gemini models to build Siri AI, Google itself has struggled to deliver a compelling experience in the home. So Apple’s opportunity lies in execution. Its more curated approach to third-party hardware has held it back, but it also means Apple arrives at this crucial moment with less technical debt and a cleaner foundation for building an AI-powered smart home.
This will be the next level for the smart home; with reliable data and context, your home could know who’s in it, where they are, and what they need, and, combined with knowing the status of every device, become proactive. For example, it could alert you that the oven is on and no one is home, suggest turning off the AC when a window is left open, and route messages and notifications to the room you’re in.
A smart home isn’t just about the devices you put in it. It’s about making them work together
This is still a distant promise, however. Today, Apple Home has significant limitations: it doesn’t support every type of home device (no fridges, washing machines, or EV chargers); it can’t control every feature of many device types; and its automations are limited compared to the competition (notably lacking conditional programming options inside the app). All this makes the Home app very easy to use, but extremely underpowered.
With Siri AI, Apple could unlock many of those capabilities via voice instead of building complicated menu interfaces. You could just tell Siri what you want your smart home to do. Alexa Plus offers this with the ability to create routines using your voice; Gemini for Home lets you use natural language in its Home app chatbot to set up automations; and many smart home companies are adopting AI in their apps to cut through UI complexity and make devices and features easier to use.
A big question remains: do people really want a smart home? Many of us have spent years frustrated with systems that hold so much promise but routinely fail to deliver, leaving us spending weekends troubleshooting why the garage door won’t open. The truly dedicated have turned to Home Assistant, a powerful platform that can do almost anything you want, if you’re willing to do the work. But for most people, beyond a few solutions to specific problems, the smart home just isn’t worth it.
Apple can’t make everything for the smart home, but it can make sure that everything works with its platform.
To win in the smart home and bring the category mainstream, Apple needs more than just great hardware; it needs a superior software experience that makes the smart home easy to use. It needs to integrate seamlessly with third-party devices and deliver a consistent, reliable experience, relying on local control wherever possible and making sure products just work.
Apple is reportedly partnering with LG and others to develop products for an “Apple Home Collection” that will add a layer of Apple polish to the smart home experience. While this might sound like going back to the walled garden of the HomeKit days, Matter ensures interoperability with other platforms. Apple can’t make everything for the smart home, but it can make sure that everything works with its platform.
Most crucially, Apple will need to double down on its commitment to privacy and data security, especially as it opens the home to Apple Intelligence’s cloud-based capabilities. If Apple can deliver on all of this, its highly anticipated smart home display might justify its price. But the real test will be whether Siri can make the smart home live up to its promise.
articles.summary:
Apple is hosting a dedicated smart home event in New York City on October 13th, where it is expected to unveil a new AI-powered smart display device.

### Key Points
- Apple is reportedly launching a 6-inch smart display, potentially named HomeView, featuring a touchscreen, facial recognition, and FaceTime capabilities.
- The new hardware is expected to run on a brand-new homeOS integrated with Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.
- The device is rumored to carry a $350 price point and will serve as a central hub for the Apple Home ecosystem.
- Apple is reportedly partnering with manufacturers like LG to develop a curated "Apple Home Collection" of compatible smart devices.
- The company aims to address long-standing smart home challenges by leveraging the Matter and Thread interoperability standards.

### Why it Matters
This event marks Apple’s most significant attempt to compete with Amazon and Google in the smart home market by shifting focus from simple hardware to AI-driven automation. If successful, the integration of Apple Intelligence could transform the smart home from a collection of disconnected gadgets into a proactive, user-aware ecosystem.

articles.title: Kindle Aluminum Review (2026): Gorgeous, but Expensive
articles.author: Nena Farrell
articles.content:
Nice compact size for smaller hands or reading on the go. Aluminum back makes the e-reader heavier, but not so heavy it's uncomfortable. Colors are beautiful. Double the storage of the plastic version. Compatible with new Kindle Click remote. Aluminum is ad-free (plastic version can be ad-free if you pay extra).
TIRED
Expensive for the least amount of features in a Kindle. No warm light, and no auto-adjusting light like you'll get on the aluminum version of other Kindles. Not compatible with Kindle Page Turn Cover.
The Kindle Aluminum has no right to be this beautiful.
Amazon announced a new Kindle lineup at the start of the month, with new versions of the Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft. The base Kindle is the first one available, with both a plastic version and an aluminum version. It's simply named the Kindle Aluminum, while the aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft are now the new Signature Editions with extra features (like wireless charging, an auto-adjusting front light, and a couple AI features).
The Kindle Aluminum only offers the AI features compared to the Signature Editions, while also including a different body, 32 GB of storage, and no lock screen ads. It's not really enough to validate the price change, yet still I find myself loving it.
Notably, it comes in two colors, Seaglass Green and Alpine Sky. The latter is currently sitting just a few inches away from me as I write this, glinting in the sunlight. It's the shade of blue I had hoped the MacBooks would be when Apple released its Sky Blue color in 2025, and every single reader friend I've shown it to has said they want it for the color alone. Even my editor, who strongly prefers physical books (which is hilarious given that she edits my ever-growing list of e-reader reviews, including this one), said just looking at my photos made her want one.
It's a smart move on Amazon's part. There's little reason to upgrade your Kindle if you already have one, but most generations only came in black. The last generation just had one color for the Kindle and one for the Paperwhite. Now, with the base Kindle, you have two colors of the plastic version (the classic black and Ube purple) and the aforementioned green or blue aluminum—these options could have plenty of existing Kindle owners champing at the bit to upgrade.
But it's hard to say it's worth it just for the color, since you could always buy a case instead. It's not a bad device, and there are some improvements—just not enough to justify the price tag.
New Body, Same System
The 12th-generation Kindle still has the same 6-inch screen, but the device's overall form factor has changed. The screen is flush with the rest of the body now, rather than sitting indented, and the new Kindle body is actually a quarter of an inch shorter than the 2024 Kindle's. That sounds like a small increment (and it is!), but having both devices side-by-side, it was easy to spot. The new Kindle also felt like it fit better in my palm, perhaps due to the smoother aluminum backing.
It's also heavier, thanks to the backing. Amazon says the Kindle Aluminum is 5.7 ounces, while the plastic 2026 Kindle is 4.9 ounces. (The 2024 plastic Kindle is 5.56 ounces.) Despite the tiny difference in weight between the 2024 Kindle and the new aluminum version, the aluminum felt palpably heavier to me—almost as if felt like my hand was putting more effort into holding it up. I double-checked on my kitchen scale, and it really is only a 0.2-ounce difference. I had my husband try both models, and he agreed that the aluminum felt heavier and was surprised at how small the difference really was. I think the smaller frame makes the weight sit a little differently.
Opening the 2026 Kindle Aluminum sends you to the same interface as any other Kindle. You'll have a homepage and your library page, and the same set of menus by tapping the right-hand corner dots or swiping down from the top of the page. I did find that while the page-turn speed seemed nearly identical, the new Kindle opened up books much faster than the 2024 Kindle. On the latter, I always had to wait a handful of seconds for my latest Kindle Unlimited read to open (I'll own up to it currently being Verity, my first and very likely last Colleen Hoover book), but the 2026 Kindle near-instantly opened it each time.
The other difference turned out to be the front lights. While neither model has a warm-color front light, the Kindle Aluminum's light tone seemed a touch warmer than the bright-blue tinge of the 2024 Kindle. It was still too blue to comfortably read in dark mode before bed, but side by side, I could see an improvement. It's hard to tell in my photo below, but I know I'm not hallucinating after seeing multiple similar photos already uploaded to the Kindle's Amazon reviews.
Colorful Cost
Ultimately, you don't need this Kindle if you already have one, and $190 is a steep price to pay for a model that doesn't even have a warm option for the front light. The real draw here remains the color body, and Amazon has done a good job with this. My TikTok feed is full of e-reader fans talking about the Ube shade, while the shine of the Alpine Sky is one I would've been eyeing had I not ended up reviewing it. I also like that the aluminum body really does feel like an upgrade when I hold it in my hands.
Amazon might be trying to take a page from Apple's playbook for the iPhone, encouraging you to upgrade your Kindle every two years for the new colors, the way superfans update their smartphones. While Kindle has a much lower cost of entry, that's because a smartphone comes with many more features and upgrades. The Kindle will always have one use: as an e-reader that shows you books. Unlike the second- to third-gen Kindle Scribe update, Kindle isn't providing a new homepage experience, though you will get two of the AI-powered features the Scribes have (Story So Far, to recap where you left off in a story, and Ask This Book—coming soon, to ask about a story). You aren't even getting the auto-adjusting light that aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft will have.
It's a good gift for Christmas for someone who already has everything, or an excuse to finally upgrade your own Kindle if it's starting to lag. But you might also want to wait and see if the Paperwhite or Colorsoft Signature Editions are the way to go instead, especially since only those two models will be compatible with the new Kindle Page Turn Cover ($80) that will give you on-device page-turn buttons. Neither the 2026 Kindle Aluminum nor the plastic version will be compatible with this accessory, making it even harder to justify upgrading, but they will at least work with the Kindle Click remote ($35).
Again, this isn't a bad Kindle. The faster book openings and slightly warmer (though still not actually warm) front light, and double the storage make it a legitimate upgrade to the 2024 model. If you don't already have a Kindle, it's not a bad choice if you want to get one of the prettiest models available. It's up to you if that's worth spending almost $200 on.
You'll likely be just as happy with the plastic Ube version and spend between $20 and $40 less, depending on whether you want ads or not (though it does have half the storage of the aluminum model, at 16 GB). Still, this is a much higher price than these basic Kindles used to be available for. Hopefully we will see these Kindles on sale for Black Friday, but I wouldn't hold my breath for any good sales this year.
Nena Farrell is a writer and reviewer at WIRED. She primarily covers home and sleep products, smart home tech, gift guides, and parenting gear. She’s been a reviewer at WIRED since 2023, and before that was a smart home updates writer at The New York Times’ Wirecutter and an associate ... Read More
articles.summary:
Amazon has released the 12th-generation Kindle Aluminum, a premium, compact e-reader featuring 32 GB of storage and new color options, though it lacks advanced lighting and accessory compatibility.

### Key Points
- The Kindle Aluminum is available in Seaglass Green and Alpine Sky, priced at $190.
- It features a 6-inch flush screen, a 5.7-ounce aluminum body, and 32 GB of internal storage.
- Performance upgrades include faster book loading times compared to the 2024 plastic model.
- The device supports AI features like "Story So Far" but lacks auto-adjusting or warm-toned front lighting.
- It is compatible with the Kindle Click remote but does not support the new Kindle Page Turn Cover.

### Why it Matters
The introduction of premium, color-focused hardware suggests Amazon is shifting its e-reader strategy toward aesthetic appeal to encourage frequent device upgrades among existing users. However, the high price point and lack of advanced features may lead consumers to consider more functional alternatives like the Paperwhite or Colorsoft Signature Editions.

articles.title: This unofficial port brings Pixel 11's Rambler to any Android phone
articles.author: sanujb6@gmail.com (Sanuj Bhatia) , Sanuj Bhatia
articles.content:
What you need to know
- Google's Rambler uses AI to clean up voice typing, removing filler words, correcting grammar, and formatting text.
- Developer Akshay Kadam has released PixelBoard, a modified Gboard APK that enables Rambler on other Android phones.
- Users can reportedly access Rambler by installing PixelBoard and setting it as their default keyboard instead of Gboard.
If you've ever wanted to try the Pixel 11's Rambler feature on your Android phone, you can now do so, although there's a catch.
The Google Pixel 11 series launched earlier this year with several new AI features, including Magic Cue, Magic Capture, and Rambler. For those unfamiliar, Rambler is Google's new AI-powered voice typing feature that offers a much more advanced experience than the regular voice typing we've had on Android phones for years.
Similar to AI voice typing tools that have been available on desktops for a while, Rambler automatically cleans up your speech, fixes grammar and formatting, and removes filler words like "um" and "uh" to give you properly formatted text. It can also understand corrections while you're speaking, add emojis, and even rewrite your text in different tones, such as formal or casual.
Unlike traditional voice typing, though, Rambler doesn't show a live transcription of everything you're saying. Instead, once you've finished speaking and tapped the Done button, it processes your speech and returns a cleaned-up, properly formatted version of what you said.
The feature has been exclusive to the Pixel 11 series so far, but a developer has now found a way to bring it to other Android devices.
Developer Akshay Kadam has shared a modified version of Google's Gboard app, called PixelBoard, on GitHub. The developer has patched the Gboard APK to enable Rambler on Android phones that don't officially support the feature.
According to the developer, you can install the modified APK on your Android device and switch your default keyboard from Gboard to PixelBoard to access Rambler without needing a Pixel 11.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
That said, PixelBoard isn't an official Google app, and installing modified APK files always carries security and privacy risks. There's also no guarantee that Rambler will continue working through this method. Since the feature is officially exclusive to the Pixel 11 series, Google could block the workaround through a future Gboard or server-side update.
But if you're curious about Rambler, the developer's GitHub project offers an unofficial way to try the feature without buying a Pixel 11. Just keep in mind that you're installing a modified keyboard at your own risk.
Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. He began his journey with a Nokia Lumia and later dived deep into Android and iPhone. He's been writing about tech since 2018, with bylines at Pocketnow, Android Police, Pocket-Lint, and MakeUseOf. When he's not testing gadgets, he's either sipping chai, watching football, or playing cricket.
