In a survey that PINE64 took of 3079 PinePhone users in January 2022, 39.3% selected Phosh as their favorite interface, compared to 15.5% for Sxmo/Swmo, 15.0% for Plasma Mobile and 6.7% for Lomiri (formerly Unity8). Despite Phosh only starting its development in April 2018, more users preferred it over Lomiri and Plasma Mobile, which have been under development since March 2013 and July 2015, respectively. Purism’s strategy of using the existing infrastructure and applications from GNOME allowed the tiny company to create a usable interface faster than other competing interfaces.
It is surprising that Phosh became the most popular mobile Linux interface, considering that the Qt toolkit and KDE had such a head start over GTK and GNOME in supporting mobile environments. Qt Quick was introduced with Qt 5.1 in June 2013 to make Qt controls adaptive for small screens, and Qt Mobile was introduced in December 2013 to make them cross-platform, and KDE’s Kirigami library for adaptive applications was introduced in March 2016. GTK didn’t gain similar abilities until 2019 with libhandy and GNOME didn’t have an answer to Kirigami until libadwaita was introduced in 2021.
Phosh has some glaring limitations. Its default Squeekboard keyboard is basic and kludgy. Only in 2025 did Phosh gain an alternative keyboard with word correction and word completion, plus the ability to select from multiple characters by long pressing a key. The desktop mode in Phosh to output video to an external monitor or projector has a very limited interface. Phosh has no camera app, and most installations rely on Megapixels developed by Martijn Braam for the PinePhone or its Millipixels fork developed by Purism for the Librem 5. Millipixels only gained basic support for auto-focus and the ability to shoot video in January 2023.
Phosh doesn’t have the three buttons at the bottom or the swipe gestures from Android that most people are used to. Plasma Mobile’s interface is much closer to the familiar Android interface, and it is nicer visually. Phosh’s interface is much simplier. It doesn’t use system navigation buttons and has fewer configuration options than Plasma Mobile. A swipe from the bottom displays Phosh’s Overview screen where apps can be opened or closed. A swipe from the top displays a Quick-Setting panel, notifications, and buttons in the top corners to lock or turn off the phone.
Phosh became the more popular interface, partly because Purism was paying developers to work on it, so it was more stable, whereas Plasma Mobile was more prone to stalls and crashes. Plasma relies on hardware acceleration from the GPU to speed up its interface, which isn’t supported by the drivers for the A64 and i.MX 8M Quad in the PinePhone and Librem 5, whereas Phosh is faster and more responsive just using software rendering. Phosh also requires less RAM, although it does run more background processes that use more CPU.
Phosh succeeded because its close adherence to a common desktop stack made it easier to package and distribute in different distros. Phosh was first adopted by postmarketOS (now Nura) in September 2018, just a two months after Purism first debuted it. The close ties between the Phosh developers and Debian helped get Phosh packaged into Debian in February 2020, where it became the basis of the new Mobian distro. Phosh allowed Debian, Arch, Manjaro, Fedora, OpenSUSE and NixOS to become mobile distros for the first time, which in turn encouraged Linux application developers to start testing their software in a mobile interface to see how it functioned on smaller screens. Because Phosh didn’t stay isolated in one Linux distro, it attracted more volunteers to help develop the software and work on porting it.
Over time, Plasma Mobile has followed Phosh’s example and increasingly unified with its Plasma desktop stack. Originally the Plasma Mobile stack was quite different from the standard desktop Plasma stack, since Plasma Mobile was based on the oFono telephony library and could be run either on the standard Linux kernel or on the Halium Project, which allows Plasma Mobile to run in an LXC container on top of an Android kernel and drivers, and using libhybris to translate its Linux calls to libc into Android’s Bionic. Over time the KDE has jettisoned parts of Plasma Mobile to unify it with its desktop stack. In December 2020, KDE announced that it would get rid of Halium and only run on a Linux kernel, because that change would allow Plasma Mobile to employ a traditional Linux userspace without blobs and upgrade their KWin composer. A year later in December 2021, Plasma Mobile announced that it was switching from the oFono library to ModemManager, because it was more stable and better maintained than oFono. Finally, in February 2026, Plasma Mobile announced it would be switching from the Maliit on-screen keyboard to the new Plasma Keyboard. Over time, KDE has incorporated Kirigami into more of its standard applications, so it doesn’t need two different applications for Plasma and Plasma Mobile.
The unification of the mobile and desktop stacks made it easier for Plasma Mobile to follow Phosh’s example in getting packaged and incorporated into all the major Linux desktop distributions, so they could also be used on mobile devices. Nearly every major distro started testing its code on the PinePhone, which helped get more people testing and contributing to Phosh and Plasma Mobile.
Despite the fact that these two interfaces have fewer developers than desktop GNOME and desktop Plasma, they have don’t need nearly as much manpower because they can piggy back on the desktop stack and the convergent apps, so they can thrive with much less dev work and maintenance than big siloed codebases like Ubuntu Touch, Firefox OS, Tizen, webOS, etc.
Sxmo (Simple X Mobile) has followed simple strategy of building on top an existing deskop stack. It was created by Miles Alan, as a “collection of simple programs and shell scripts” on top of Sway and its wlroots library. It was first released in February 2020, and quickly became the second most popular interface on the PinePhone due to its light-weight and simple design, which made it easy to customize. Sxmo has been incorporated into the mobile distros (postmarketOS, Mobian and DanctNIX), but the desktop distros haven’t adopted it, which has limited its reach.
UBport’s Lomiri interface is faster and more responsive and consumes less RAM than Phosh and Plasma Mobile, but it was originally isolated in Ubuntu Touch. Canonical spent years developing its Unity8 interface, which is based on Qt Quick and used in Ubuntu Touch. The UBports community renamed the interface as Lomiri in February 2020. UBports has followed a similar strategy of trying to attract more people to its Lomiri interface by getting it incorporated into the major distros. UBports modified Ubuntu Touch and the Lomiri interface so they could run on either Halium or a standard Linux kernel, and switched to using more standardized libraries that were easier to upgrade over time. Nonetheless its small number of volunteers has struggled to maintain its huge codebase, and update it to new versions of Qt.
Despite the head start of Plasma Mobile and Lomiri, they stayed isolated for longer in KDE Neon and Ubuntu Touch. In contrast, Phosh got adopted almost immediately by postmarketOS, and once it got packaged by Debian in early 2020, most of the other major distros quickly adopted it. When postmarketOS was first released in May 2017, it used Weston, which is Wayland’s reference compositor, but within the first 100 days of its existence, postmarketOS adopted Plasma Mobile. However, postmarketOS chose to ship its PinePhone Community Edition with Phosh due to its greater stability.

Unlike in the past, when mobile Linux interfaces were isolated in a few distros, many distros now support Phosh, Plasma Mobile and Lomiri. Because mobile Linux is no longer isolated and locked into silos controlled by large companies, such as Nokia, Samsung, LG, Mozilla and Canonical, it has a much greater chance of succeeding and attracted contributors than it did in the past. Because Phosh and Plasma Mobile and Sxmo are based on using existing software stacks that are maintained by outside organizations, they are much less likely to be abandoned, as happened with Firefox OS, or to ossify and fade into obscurity, as happened with Hildon.
PINE64 was founded as a crowd-funding campaign in October 2015 by TL Lim and Johnson Jeng to develop a single board computer based on the Allwinner A64 processor. The company based in Hong Kong focuses on producing economical Linux hardware devices. It gets around the high costs of developing software by just producing the hardware and then invites the community to develop the software for its devices. By allying with various different Linux distros, PINE64 initially had a great deal of success.
PINE64 probably shipped over 100,000 PinePhones, which greatly stimulated the development of mobile Linux. The release of the PinePhone led to the creation of the Mobian (Mobile Debian) and DanctNIX (based on Arch ARM) distros and inspired the creation of the Sxmo interface. The PinePhone helped Plasma Mobile decide that it only needed to run on a Linux stack and pushed UBports to add support for running on a Linux kernel. It also caused many of the major distros to work on porting to a mobile device for the first time.
PINE64 played an important service for the community by getting cheap hardware into people’s hands so they develop software for that hardware, but it made the fundamental mistake of focusing on the distros, which only works if the hardware already has kernel support and good free/open source drivers. Drew DeVault, the lead developer of Sway and one of the volunteer developers who worked on the PinePhone, observed that PINE64 was putting the cart before the horse, by helping to finance the packaging work in particular distos, rather than first paying developers to work on the booting and driver development, that would have benefitted all the distros.
Because PINE64 chose hardware for the PinePhone that was mostly already supported by FOSS drivers, it was able to attract a large number of distros to work on the phone. Volunteer developer Ondřej Jirman (aka “mega” or “megi”) created a custom Linux kernel for the PinePhone. Volunteers at UBports did the initial work on bringing up the hardware. Arnaud Ferraris (aka “a-wai”) at Mobian developed the telephony stack using the eg25-manager in userspace. Martijn Braam at postmarketOS worked on the camera. PINE64 initially released a series of five development batches of the PinePhone, which had different distros preinstalled (Ubuntu Touch, postmarketOS with Phosh, Manjaro with Phosh, Manjaro with Plasma Mobile and Mobian with Phosh). For each phone sold, PINE64 donated $10 to the distro which provided the software. After that, PINE64 planned to let the buyer select which distro to support by selecting the distro’s logo to display on the back plate of the PinePhone’s case.
Nonetheless, there were arguments among the different distros behind the scenes over the design of the hardware projects. PINE64’s founder, TL Lim, grew frustrated and decided to just ship PINE64’s devices with one distro and one interface preinstalled. Given the complexity of trying to work with so many different distros, this wasn’t an unreasonable decision, but it had to be handled with care to not alienate the other distros. Unfortunately, Lim chose to only ship PINE64 devices with Manjaro and Plasma Mobile preinstalled. PINE64’s own poll of PinePhone users showed that Phosh was the most popular interface, but it was controlled by Purism, a competitor to PINE64. Plasma Mobile wasn’t a bad choice, since it was a community-based interface that needed corporate support. Manjaro, however, was a very poor choice, since it wasn’t doing any software dev work and has been widely criticized for its bad practice of shipping software in development that is known to be broken, which creates more work and public backlash for the projects developing the software.
Many of the crucial volunteers who worked on the PinePhone were burned out by the time that development on the PinePhone Pro started. They were frustrated by the internal arguments and the fact that PINE64 had shifted from sharing revenue with many distros to only paying Manjaro, rather than the people who were doing the necessary dev work. The PinePhone Pro’s hardware required quite a bit of software dev work to support it. In August 2022, Martijn Braam at postmarketOS publicly broke up with PINE64 due to its bad decisions in favor of Manjaro. PINE64’s response failed to address Braam’s frustrations, and Drew DeVault posted that “PINE64 has let its community down.” Most of the volunteer developers stopped collaborating with PINE64, so the community-based company didn’t have the manpower to do the necessary software development for its new hardware. Most distros weren’t willing to work on a phone that couldn’t even properly boot. Thousands of people bought the PinePhone Pro after it was released in December 2021, expecting that eventually it would become a functional device, but it still had major software problems when its sales were cancelled in August 2025. The failure of the PinePhone Pro illustrates that PINE64 had its priorities backwards by focusing on one distro that mainly does packaging work, rather than focusing on the booting and kernel work.
Another of the problems was that PINE64 sent out its free hardware samples to the same small number of volunteers. By the time that the PinePhone Pro started its development, those volunteers were overwhelmed by all the new hardware that PINE64 was releasing, which all needed serious software dev work to ever be functional. With so many projects needing attention, the volunteers couldn’t focus their energy on any one device, so all of them got neglected.
PINE64 charges such low prices for its hardware, that it doesn’t have the necessary funds to pay for serious software dev work. However, its revenue sharing model with the distros was working to convince talented people associated with those distros to do the hard work of supporting its hardware. Then, PINE64 undermined its whole community development model by deciding that it would only sell its hardware with one distro and one interface preinstalled, and its decision to only share its revenue with that one distro. Then, PINE64 made matters worse by only listening to Manjaro in how it designed its hardware, which alienated many of the volunteers from other distros that it needed to do the software dev work. Once the best volunteers abandoned PINE64, the company hasn’t been able to complete the development of the PinePhone Pro, PineNote, PineTab2 and many of its other projects, so the people who ordered these devices are unlikely to ever be able to use them as fully functional devices.
Rather than sharing revenue with many different distros, PINE64 should have used any profits that it generated to pay developers to work on the drivers and kernel support for the hardware. It could have taken a community-based approach by observing who was making progress, and helping to finance their work. Because the Allwinner A64 already had decent free/open source drivers, volunteers were able to fill in the gaps with the PinePhone. However, many of the kernel changes that they made never got upstreamed to mainline Linux, which PINE64 could have required if it were paying for that work.
PINE64 also could have directed its revenue sharing program to help finance development work that would benefit all users of PinePhone, regardless of which distro they chose, such as Martijn Braam’s work on the Megapixels camera app or Biktorgj’s work on freeing the EG25-G modem firmware. Given that Phosh, Plasma Mobile, Lomiri and Sxmo/Swmo were being packaged in many different distros, it would have been better to pay people to work on developing those mobile interfaces than giving money to the distros. There are plenty of volunteers in the community who were willing to work on porting distros to the PinePhone, but there are far fewer people who are willing to do difficult driver and software dev work in their spare time.
After the initial enthusiasm for the Librem 5, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro in 2020-21, there was a noticeable drop in people’s interest in Linux phones. The number of posts about the Librem 5 and PinePhone on Reddit and the Purism and PINE64 forums reduced in 2022-25. The subsequent announcements of new Linux phones, namely the F(x)tec Pro1 X with Sailfish OS and Ubuntu Touch, the Volla phones with Ubuntu Touch, FuriLabs FLX1/s/s+, the Jolla C2 with Sailfish OS, Liberux NEXX, Commodore Callback 8020 and Mecha Comet, haven’t generated nearly as much public interest and community engagement as the announcements of the Librem 5, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. This difference is partly due to the fact that Purism and PINE64 were established companies that were already shipping Linux devices and they had community forums and Subreddits where people could gather and discuss the upcoming devices.
Nonetheless, I suspect that many of the people who bought the Librem 5 and PinePhone had a similar experiences to mine which dampened their enthusiasm for Linux phones over time. When both of those phones first arrived, they were fascinating devices for geeks like me, who had been playing around with Linux for years on their desktop PCs. I had a blast flashing different distros on the PinePhone and I frequently downloaded the latest version of PureOS and reflashed my Librem 5. I ran benchmarks on the two phones and eagerly followed the dev work to add support for the phones’ hardware. I had spent years waiting for the Librem 5, and after it arrived, I followed the development of Phosh and Adwaita by the Purism developers, like I was rooting for my favorite sports team. I considered the development of Phosh and Plasma Mobile to be the most exciting thing that was happening in the Linux world, and I enjoyed trying out new versions of the interfaces to see what was new in each release.
The first year after the Librem 5 and PinePhone were released were exciting times. I was so intrigued by the phones that I looked up every component on the Librem 5 and PinePhone schematics and documented them on the projects’ wikis. However, each time I flashed a new distro on the PinePhone to try it out, I only played with the phone for a day or two, before it went back in the drawer on my desk. I took the PinePhone apart and admired how it was designed, but I never used the phone for very long before I put it down. Its performance was poor. It took a long time to load apps and there was a noticeable delay in the interface. I also found it distracting to use the phone when the screen was dimmed or the battery was low, because of the noticeable flicker on the screen. I considered pulling out the soldering iron to implement a fix that would speed up the Flash memory storage, but I feared that I might accidentally ruin the board. I expected that PINE64 would issue an new version of the PinePhone that would fix the problems, but instead PINE64 dismissed the screen flicker as a problem and hasn’t changed the eMMC’s voltage from 3.3 to 1.8 volts, which would have increased its sequential read speed from 55 to 125 MB/s. I was also annoyed that PINE64 provided no way to communicate with its hardware developers, so I wasn’t able to get errors fixed that I found in the PinePhone schematics.
Unlike the Pinephone which I rarely used, I kept using the Librem 5, because its better CPU and memory performance made its interface much more responsive than the PinePhone. Nonetheless, the Librem 5’s screen and aluminum frame got hot, since Purism used thermal paste to join the i.MX 8M Quad to the LCD’s backplate to dissipate the processor’s heat through the screen and aluminum frame. I often felt like I was walking around with a heater in my pocket. The battery drained fast, so I was constantly having to charge the Librem 5.
Eventually the Purism developers got the Librem 5’s camera to work, and I tried out each new version of the Millipixels app. It was fun playing with the camera and I learned a lot about how cameras work trying to adjust the settings to get a good photo. However, the Librem 5 took a long time to process each photo in software after taking a picture, since its i.MX 8M Quad processor lacked an image signal processor and hardware encoder in the VPU. It also took me way too long fiddling with the Millipixels’ settings for me to rely on the camera. Whenever I wanted to make sure that I would get a decent photo, I pulled out my Xiaomi Redmi Note 7 running LineageOS to take the photo. Eventually it was possible to shoot video on the Librem 5 at a low resolution and frame rate, but it took so long to process the video and the quality was so limited, that I never bothered using it.
In the end, the PinePhone sat most of the time in a drawer in my desk, and the Librem 5 sat charging on my desk. They were good entertainment for the geek in me, but I didn’t use either of them as my primary phone. Many of the early adopters appear to have had similar experiences with their Linux phones. It was hard to justify buying another Linux phone, when there was already one sitting unused in the drawer. Many people were unwilling to take a chance on another Linux phone after witnessing how the community developers abandoned PINE64 in 2022, and software development stalled for the PinePhone Pro and how Purism refused to refund cancelled orders for the Librem 5.
When FuriLabs announced its upcoming FLX1 in June 2024, it solved many of the problems with the Librem 5 and PinePhone. It contained a 6nm MediaTek Dimensity 900, which was powerful enough shoot video and run 3D games with Vulkan. It offers three hardware privacy switches and multi-booting to run multiple operating systems on the phone. The phone’s software was developed by Bardia Moshiri, who is the lead developer of Droidian, which runs Phosh in a Debian-based distro on top of Halium with an Android kernel. It was based on well-supported projects and software which had already been developed, so its costs would be low, but it had an experienced developer to provide software support. In other words, it would avoid the high costs that troubled the Librem 5 and the lack of software support that bedeviled the PinePhone Pro. People report that the FLX1 and its following FLX1s and FLX1s+ variants work well, but the Linux phone is not well-known and appears to have gotten a limited number of orders. The company’s forum has been frozen and there has been limited activity on the Droidian forum, indicating that the phone has gained little traction in the Linux community.

In January 2025, Liberux, a startup based in Madrid, Spain, announced its upcoming NEXX Linux phone based on the RK3588S with specs to make nerds salivate: 4×2.4GHz Cortex-A76, 4x Cortex-A55, Mali-G610 MP4 GPU, 32GB LPDDR4X RAM, 256GB eMMC, 5G modem and 3 hardware kill switches. In June 2025, Liberux started the crowdfunding for the phone, and a couple days later announced a modular and open architecture that would allow the RAM board with an FPC connector to be upgraded up to 32GB, the eMMC board with a standard socket to be upgraded up to 512GB, and the cellular modem with a custom adapter board to be replaced/upgraded. The price varied between €790 and €1310, depending on the selected configuration. In addition, the NEXX would have two USB-C 3.1 ports to facilitate the phone being used a convergent desktop PC and an AW8737SCSR amplifier and a 3.5mm audio jack for better analog audio.
The NEXX was a revolutionary design, promising to be the first phone in history with two USB ports and the first one with the RAM and eMMC on separate boards, so it could be upgraded and connected like a normal PC. Liberux was attempting to offer the first truly convergent smartphone that had the right software and hardware to replace a desktop PC, yet it hardly generated any headlines in the tech press. It only got 120 pre-orders in a month, which generated a tenth of the $1.7 million in crowdfunding that it needed. When its crowdfunding campaign failed, Liberux reported that it was negotiating with investors for raise the funds to build a prototype. However, its last post on the company’s Mastadon account was in November 2025 about “moving forward with new self-funding.” After 11 months of silence, it is looking increasingly doubtful that the NEXX will ever come to market.
There is more hope for the Dawndrums Divine D. phone, which is being produced by a startup in Tunisia. The startup has continued to make slow progress according to its Mastodon posts. They are now on the second revision of their main board and have produced a breakout board for debugging it. They are developing their own distro known as DawnOS, which is based on Mobian and planning to support both the Phosh and Plasma Mobile interfaces. They are asking for donations, but appear to be largely self funded at this point. Like the NEXX, the Divine D. also promises to be an outstanding convergent phone, supporting up to 32GB RAM and offering a separate HDMI port for video out. It also offers a LoRa (long-range radio) chip, and a pogo pin interface to add accessories to the phone.
While the failed crowdfunding of the Liberux NEXX and the limited sales of the FuriLabs FLX1 would suggest that there isn’t much hope for Linux phones, it is important to keep in mind that these phones were poorly advertised and produced by unknown startups that had no prior track record, so people were reluctant to order them. Bitter experience with the Librem 5 refunds, the failures of the PinePhone Pro, and all the cancelled Linux mobile devices over the years, such as the Ubuntu Edge in 2013, the Firefox OS phones in 2015, the Jolla Tablet in 2015 and the Necunos NC_1 in 2019, has taught Linux enthusiasts to be cautious about crowdfunding mobile devices.
However, there are reasons to believe that there is quite a bit of pent-up demand for mobile Linux, and it only requires the right kind of promotion and a company with a credible track record to unlock it. Ironically, the company demonstrating that people still want to use Linux phones is tiny Jolla, which has somehow managed to survive over the years.
The Finnish engineers who used to work on Nokia’s MeeGo founded their own company named Jolla Oy in 2011 to keep developing that code as Sailfish OS. They took the FOSS parts of MeeGo and added their proprietary Silica interface based on Qt QML, which imitates the Swipe UI that Nokia had developed for MeeGo on the N900/N9. They also licensed the proprietary Alien Dalvik from Myriad Group to run Android apps inside Linux, and now markets it as AppSupport, which has been updated to run more recent versions of AOSP in an LXC container. Jolla deserves credit for developing libhybris and helping to maintain much of the code developed by Nokia, including the oFono telephony library and the Maliit virtual keyboard. Remarkably, the small Finnish company managed to survive nearly going bankrupt in late 2015, when it cancelled its crowdfunded Jolla Tablet, and was only able to return half of the money to the customers who pre-ordered the tablet.
After killing off the original company in 2024, because it was majority owned by Russian investors, who were politically toxic due to the war in Ukraine, Jolla reemerged under a new company named JollaBoys that bought the old company’s assets from Jolla Oy. The new Jolla company has returned to the business of selling hardware. Jolla announced its Jolla C2 Community Phone in May 2024, and started delivering them four months later, which helped reestablish the credibility of the company. When Jolla started taking preorders for its new Jolla Phone on December 5, 2025, it sold out its crowdfunding goal of 2000 phones within the first 48 hours and 5000 phones within the first week. People were pre-ordering the Jolla Phone without having seen any reviews of the phone and not even knowing what processor it would contain. The phone, which initially cost $499 and now costs was €679, was marketed as containing 12GB RAM, 256GB storage, a user-replaceable battery and a physical privacy switch. Jolla’s advertising for the phone clearly struck a chord with European consumers, which proclaimed it to be a “Do It Together (DIT) Linux phone, shaped by the people who use it.” The Finnish company emphasized the independence of the phone from the rest of the mobile phone industry, stating on the order page: “The Jolla Phone is not based on Big Tech technology. It is governed by European privacy thinking and a community-led model.”
Jolla has sold 15,000 units of its phone as of August 2026 just by taking pre-orders for production batches from its web site, and it probably could have sold far more units if it had paid for advertising, expanded beyond the European market, and kept the phone in stock, so customers didn’t have to wait months for the next production batch. Clearly, there is an untapped market of people who are dissatisfied with the reigning Android/iOS duopoly.
Today the use of Linux is growing on the desktop. Many people are installing Linux on their PCs, because they have become disgusted by how Microsoft has turned Windows into an advertising platform for surveillance capitalism and a vehicle for AI slop. Rather than buying new PCs, a growing number of people have decided to install Linux, because support for Windows 10 has ended and they can’t upgrade their old PCs to Windows 11 due to Microsoft’s arbitrary TPM restrictions.
Likewise, many people are equally disenchanted with Android and iOS on their phones. More people have grown distrustful of the surveillance capitalism which undergirds the Android market and the restrictions and rising prices of Apple’s “walled garden” on the iPhone, yet the options to escape the smartphone duopoly keep shrinking. In the past, people who wanted to gain some control over their digital lives could unlock the bootloader on their phone and install an AOSP derivative such as LineageOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS or GrapheneOS, however the mobile phone industry is increasingly shutting off this escape valve.
Every year there are fewer Android phone models on the market which allow the bootloader to be unlocked. The rise of Chinese brands, which now control roughly 60% of the global smartphone market, has driven many of the traditional phones brands out of the market which did allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Many of the phone brands that were mod-friendly, such as LG, BQ, LeEco, WileyFox, Essential and Razer, are now gone from the market, and other mod-friendly brands like Sony and HTC now have so few sales that they are no longer relevant in the global smartphone market. Huawei stopped allowing its bootloaders to be unlocked in 2018. In the last couple years, Samsung, ASUS and Realme all followed Huawei’s bad example and no longer allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Xiaomi, which rose to fame as a mod-friendly brand, has recently implemented so many restrictions to obtain its unlock codes, that it is unlikely that modders will bother porting custom ROMs to future Xiaomi models.
As noted in my article on LineageOS statistics, the brands which have good policies for bootloader unlocking has shrunk from 42.5% to about 7% of the global smartphone market over the last couple years. The brands which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked (without major restrictions like Xiaomi) only sold about 87 million phones in 2025, including Lenovo/Motorola (60M), Google (12M), OnePlus (11.6M), Nothing (2M), GigaSet (>1M), Sony (400k), Fairphone (145k), SHIFT (10k), Teracube, Volla and Brax. Together those brands only represent 7% of the 1245.5 million total smartphones sold in 2025.
However, that is an overestimate, since most phone models never get good custom ROMs made for them. A good portion of Motorola and Google phones are sold through carriers, and many carriers like Verizon don’t allow their phones to ever be unlocked, even if they are no longer under contract. MediaTek Dimensity and UNISOC Tiger processors have gained market share in recent years, and those chipmakers don’t publish the source code for their kernels like Qualcomm does for its Snapdragon processors. A few brands that use MediaTek SoC’s, such as Motorola, Xiaomi, Volla, Gigaset, TeraCube and Brax, do publish their kernel code, but that code for many other MediaTek phones will never get published, nor will custom ROMs be made for them. UNISOC processors are basically black boxes for the modding community. The bootloaders of all phones with Apple A-series, Huawei Kirin and recent Samsung Exynos processors are locked, so the modding community is restricted to just Qualcomm Snapdragon, Google Tensor and some MediaTek Dimensity processors. Motorola and Xiaomi have switched most of their budget model lines from Snapdragon to MediaTek Dimensity processors, so they are harder to mod.
Aside from the Motorola Moto G05, which was released in Jan 2025 and replaced 8 months later by the G06, there has not been a single budget phone released by a major phone maker in 2025 or 2026 that has gained official support by LineageOS. Gaining official LineageOS support is important, because many of the other custom ROMs are based on LineageOS and only port to its officially supported models. Just looking at phone models with official LineageOS support which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked, only about 20 million or 2% of smarphones sold each year are good for installing custom ROMs.
The situation is about to get much worse. Sadly, Oppo just announced that it will pull its OnePlus brand from the North American and European markets. OnePlus phones will still be sold in India and China (where the bootloader can be unlocked if the user presents an official Chinese ID card), but OnePlus is essentially gone for the modding community. Nothing, which was a rising star in the modding world, has been losing sales. The London-based company denies rumors that it will pull out of a third of the countries where it currently sells phones, but confirms that it plans to cut 100 jobs, which comprise 12% of its workforce. At any rate, none of the phones which Nothing has released in the last two years have gained official LineageOS support.
Samsung has been making it more and more difficult to mod its phones over the last decade, so the Korean company’s decision to lock the bootloader for all its phones getting its ONE UI 8 interface wasn’t a surprise, but Xiaomi’s decision to start restricting its bootloader unlock codes was a major blow for the modding community. The only major global brand left for modding is Motorola, but there are only unofficial ports available for recent Motorola models, meaning that some things don’t work correctly or security patches aren’t being provided. Motorola promises to launch phones with GrapheneOS in 2027, but they will be flagship models which probably cost over $1000 and be limited to a few select countries.
Aside from the Motorola Moto G15 (released in December 2024), people are unlikely to find a new phone where they can install an official LineageOS port for sale in Africa, most of Latin America (except Mexico) and most of Asia (except India, Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia). The only option to run a custom ROM in most of the world is to buy a used Motorola or Xiaomi phone from a couple years ago, such as the Moto G (2024), Moto G32, Moto G34, Moto G84, POCO F5, POCO F5 Pro, POCO F6 Pro or Redmi Note 13 Pro. There are more recent phones like the Moto Edge 70, which have unofficial LineageOS ports, but it is a gamble if they will ever be officially supported by LineageOS.
As Google has pushed phone makers to support their phones for longer, many companies have decided to collect more personal data from their users for better targeted advertising and for training artificial intelligences. The smartphone industry is moving away from a business model based on planned obsolescence toward one based on surveillance capitalism, and the phone makers don’t want their users to opt out of the system, so they have removed the option to unlock the bootloader and made it harder to gain root access. That way they can recoup the cost of providing more years of support for their phones by monetizing their users’ data.
In addition, Google has made it harder to maintain custom ROMs, because it has moved more and more functionality from AOSP into its proprietary libraries and services (starting with Android 4.1 in 2012), and largely abandoned the development of many of the free/open source apps in AOSP in favor of its proprietary apps. Starting with AOSP 16 in 2025, Google stopped including the device trees and driver binaries for Pixel devices in AOSP, so ROM developers no longer had target devices, where they could easily test out and adapt the latest versions of AOSP on running hardware. Now custom ROM developers have to do painful trial and error to make the device trees for Pixel phones just like all the other phone brands. Google also squashed the kernel’s commit history, which makes it very difficult for ROMs like GrapheneOS to create their own custom kernels, because they can’t easily take new features, bug fixes and security patches from Google’s kernels.
Given how the smartphone industry is locking down their hardware and pushing business models that are inimical to users’ privacy, there is increased opportunity for Linux phones to be marketed to people who want to escape the Android/iOS duopoly and surveillance capitalism.
In the past, it was much harder to bring a Linux phone to market, but now there are three viable types of Linux phones that can be brought to market, and all of them have better prospects than in the past. The first type is the pure Linux phone which runs a Linux kernel, like the Librem 5, Liberty, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. These phones previously didn’t have the processing power to offer the functionality that people expect in a smartphone. They often lacked components such image signal processors, audio digital signal processors, hardware video encoders, Vulkan graphics, neural processors and encryption engines, or they lacked the FOSS drivers to support those components. The RK3588S and the upcoming RK3668, however, will give pure Linux phones the processing power to be viable alternatives to Android and iOS phones for the first time.
The pure Linux phone is the riskiest type because it requires the most investment in engineering the hardware. Companies can’t just modify a reference phone design from Qualcomm or MediaTek or call up a phone ODM and ask them to modify one of their existing designs. They have to work with a design house or ODM that has some experience with radio frequencies to custom design a phone with 2 to 3 times more components than a standard smartphone. This means many iterations of the circuit board to get it right, and some kernel work to use all those different chips. It will take a long time to get to market, which can lead to customer complaints and reputational loss if using crowdfunding to finance the dev work.
The benefit of the pure Linux approach is that it allows for true hardware kill switches that cut the current to separate components, rather than the use of pins on an integrated mobile SoC or software to turn off the WiFi/Bluetooth, cellular modem and GPS/GNSS. The second benefit is the ability to select components that have free/open source drivers, which allows for greater software freedom and more transparency to address security and privacy concerns. The use of proprietary blobs in the drivers often prevents the kernel from being upgraded because the blobs are often only compatible with a specific kernel version number, which allows the chipmakers to dictate the lifespan of devices. Another benefit of not using a reference design from an SoC maker or an ODM is the phone maker has full control over the design and can publish the schematics and board views for the circuit boards, so the hardware is as free as the software.
In the past, Qualcomm didn’t produce powerful Internet of Things processors with Linux support, but now it is possible to build a good Linux phone based on an Internet of Things processor, like the QCM6490 or QCM8850 with an integrated cellular modem. These Dragonwing processors are not as up-to-date as the latest Snapdragon processors, but most of them receive 10 years or 15 years of software support, and many of them will eventually get partial support in mainline Linux, so they can live on with community support after they are no longer supported by Qualcomm.
The third kind of Linux phone is built on an integrated mobile SoC, which runs a standard Linux stack on top of an Android kernel using libhybris to translate glib calls to Android’s Bionic. This used to not be a good option because Android SoC’s were not supported long enough for the long development cycles and lower annual sales of Linux phones, but now it is possible for the high-end processors that are getting 8 years of software support from Qualcomm and MediaTek.
This approach is the most economical way to bring a Linux phone to market, since many phone ODMs already have reference models available and are willing to work with phone sellers to tweak those models to their specifications. It is not impossible to work with an ODM to add privacy switches to a design, as FuriLabs demonstrated with its FLX1, but it takes longer to get a custom design to market, so it is important to select an SoC that gets 7 or 8 years of software support, so the phone will enjoy a reasonable lifespan.
It is no longer necessary for Linux phone companies to expend huge amounts of capital in developing mobile Linux, because there are now three good mobile interfaces—Phosh, Plasma Mobile and Lomiri—which offer a reasonably complete complement of applications, so hardware companies don’t need to risk bankruptcy developing the software like before. Because Phosh and now Plasma Mobile are based on a well-supported desktop stack and convergent applications, they will require much less work to maintain and it is easier and less costly to keep providing software updates for the phone. Companies offering Linux phones will still need to hire developers to work on things like power management and camera support, but they don’t have to bet the farm like Purism did with the Librem 5 or provide no software support as PINE64 did with the PinePhone and PinePhone Pro.
